event: VXE 966 intermittently lost communication to XCOMM, OGCS and the aircraft web pages during ground testing at IVY Sting, over both Silvus and a wired AUX 2 connection, and was grounded and returned on RMA.
failure_mode: radio would not respond on its assigned tail-number virtual IP address, so the aircraft network was unreachable on that address; worked on the default and tail 1 addresses
contributing: congested RF environment at the test site, per engineering
earlier XCOMM replacement on this aircraft for a power bus reading fault (XKIT-5219), not shown to be related

evidence.quote: we were not able to get to the silvus virtual ip address assigned to the vehicle.
we swapped with a known good radio, and set the vIP to the assigned tail # with no issues
This happened over Silvus and a wired connection through the AUX 2 port.
I also don't think we can recreate the congested RF environment in which the issue was observed.

team_view_in_comments: we swapped with a known good radio, and set the vIP to the assigned tail # with no issues

would_settle_it.what: XCOMM and radio logs at the dropouts on Jan 26, 27 and Feb 3, to confirm the radio, not XCOMM, dropped the link, including over the wired AUX 2 path

would_settle_it.file: Silvus radio teardown or vendor report
would_settle_it.what: why the removed radio would not hold its assigned virtual IP (configuration corruption or hardware)

reasoning: At RMA the XCOMM page and IPCOMM page were reachable, but the Silvus radio's assigned virtual IP was not, while the default and tail 1 addresses worked. Swapping in a known good radio set to the same assigned address cleared the fault, and the repair quote replaced the Silvus enclosure. The swap test points at the radio, but the intermittent field symptom (including over wired AUX 2) was never reproduced, so confidence is medium.
notes: The MCM ip route / link statistics attachment shows 199 dropped receive packets on eth1 but no clear fault. Intake PDF has no text (scanned images). The wired AUX 2 dropouts are not explained by the radio swap alone. XKIT-5219 (earlier XCOMM replacement on 966 for bad ADC voltage readings) read for context only.

event: VXE-533 (75th Rangers, battery configuration) completed vertical takeoff but nose-dived and tumbled to the ground at the moment the lift motors shut off during transition to fixed wing flight, with significant damage.
failure_mode: loss of pitch control after transition: the aircraft pitched nose down as soon as the lift motors stopped, suspected elevator servo out of trim or failed
contributing: front lift props were carrying 63 and 84 percent (RF/LF) just before shutoff, suggesting a nose-down moment being held by the lift system
low groundspeed after transition (46 fps)
elevator seemed sluggish in post-crash LaunchWizard check

evidence.quote: The state machines both transitioned normally, it just nosedived once the vtol motors shut off
The front prop was still drawing current, and lack of front prop thrust wouldn’t explain that dramatic of a nose dive.
However, I will note that is did seem a bit ‘sluggish’ when prompted with the LaunchWizard.
Mostly likely explanation is servo out of trim or failure, but we cannot determine definitively.

team_view_in_comments: Mostly likely explanation is servo out of trim or failure, but we cannot determine definitively.

would_settle_it.what: lift motor loading and pitch command versus elevator deflection around the transition
the completed report linked in Issue Status, for the data review and servo findings
inspect the original elevator servo for the known servo issue Eric Brewer mentioned (gear damage, trim offset)
elevator command and position, pitch rate and cruise motor current through transition

attachments_read: 64589_Warranty RMA-001138 Noble - USASOC - Stalker Block 30 AV for VXE-533 (RMA 260312-3).pdf.md
reasoning: Customer reported loss of forward prop, but engineering logs show the front prop still drawing current, both autopilots transitioning normally, no lost link and a consistent airspeed bias, ruling out those causes. The nose-dive began as soon as the lift motors, which were holding a large share of the weight at the front, shut off, pointing at pitch control. Post-crash checks found nothing definite beyond a sluggish horizontal tail, and the tail boom was destroyed, so the elevator servo remains only the most likely candidate.
notes: The Issue Status link points to a file named VXE937Crash_VXEP1775.pptx, which may be the wrong report. RMA-944 description copies the VXE-547 fuel cell narrative and adds a short V533 note (no forward prop spin). The RMA ended in full aircraft replacement. Intake PDF has no text; maint log CSV has no data rows exported. XKIT-5360 not read (relates link to another crash).

Payload will turn off pan and tilt motors when given steering commands like Stow or Pilots window and will not return to Rate mode or move again.
No Error warning shows. Replicated in bench testing and in flight.
Camera was sent to Riga for investigation and repair.

reasoning: The fault was replicated on the bench as well as in flight, so it lies in the gimbal itself rather than the aircraft or link. No vendor finding is in the export, so the failing part inside the gimbal is not known.

failure_mode: radio swapped in from another aircraft kept its old IP configuration and IPCOMM failed to re-derive and push the 576 addresses
contributing: known fleet issue of IPCOMM boards failing to update tail numbers (VXEP-1698)

evidence.quote: Customer had swapped radios with another aircraft.
IP comm issue still exist but this specific VXEP was a separate radio (not 576) was installed and the IP comm failing to update is why they saw the wrong IPcomm

whether this IPCOMM shows the same failure to switch tail numbers as the boards in VXEP-1698

event: Fleet-wide investigation of XCOMM watchdog timer (WD) resets on Block 30 and Block 40 aircraft, seen in flight and on the bench, which leave air data stale while XCOMM reboots.
component: XCOMM 12V and 6V on-board DC-DC power converters
failure_mode: processor exception (mostly data bus errors in the UART3 transmit interrupt) followed by watchdog reset, linked to noise or power integrity from the on-board power converters
contributing: firmware changes in 6.6.1 / XCOMM 4.74 increased WD frequency; later B40 RC builds reduced them
EMI sensitivity (phone calls, open connector window to AP)
weak production burn-in (extended from 6 to 24 hours)
SD card corruption seen during the investigation

evidence.quote: Turning off all 12V and 6V converters on a XCOM with a lot of WDs (Rate ~6/hr before) eliminated them over a 3 day period.
This seems to prove on this board and (likely others) WDs are related to power converters on XCOM.
7/96 XCOMs failed burn in running the 6.6.1 release (XCOMM v4.74).
Since implemented related CAs to burn in and FW, 0 WDs in all B40 flight and ground testing since 4/1/20206.
WD related improvements (Mainly redo power converters or move off board)

team_view_in_comments: This seems to prove on this board and (likely others) WDs are related to power converters on XCOM.

would_settle_it.what: WDT Hardware Investigation deck and WD tracker sheet: WD rate by converter variant and with converters off across several boards
brown-out detection on the 3.3V line and WD rate on modified versus original boards

reasoning: Turning off the 12V and 6V converters on a board with about 6 WDs per hour eliminated them over three days, and the engineers conclude the WDs are related to the XCOM power converters. Crash dumps show mostly data bus errors on a fixed SRAM read in the UART3 transmit interrupt, consistent with a hardware or power integrity cause rather than a code bug. Firmware and burn-in changes reduced WDs but the mechanism is not pinned to one part, so this is narrowed.
notes: Ticket is still in D4 and covers many aircraft and boards (XCOM 5-6356, 5-6159, 5-6375; vehicles 882, 913 in linked tickets). Only one of the six FS2-4316 attachments (crash 207 summary) was read; VXEP-1701 (burn-in corrective action) and the other linked tickets (VXEP-1548, VXEP-1775, RMA-864, XKIT-5113) were not read. Typo in source: 4/1/20206.

event: VXE-547 (75th Rangers, fuel cell configuration) struggled in VTOL climb above 20 ft with an HLB cell imbalance warning, the operator aborted, and it drifted into the transport cases on descent, breaking a lift boom and props.
failure_mode: two HLB cells (6 and 7) sagged below 3 V under VTOL climb load, so the lift system could not hold the climb
contributing: heavy fuel cell configuration at 40 lb take-off weight
aircraft drifted about 50 ft during abort descent into the cases

evidence.quote: Cells 6 and 7 in the Hybrid Lift Battery underperformed during the VTOL assent phase and as a result, the aircraft achieved a semi-controlled decent into the aircraft cases.
Voltage in cells 6 and 7 drop below 3
VTOL autopilot, VTOL Motors, Electronic Speed Controllers (ESC’s) were all operating within design specifications.
Remove the Hybrid Lift Battery associated with this incident (S/N: 02-2768).
HLB FAILURE- READY FOR QUOTE- WARRANTY

team_view_in_comments: HLB cell imbalance is an Ann Arbor power system issue.

would_settle_it.what: cell capacity and internal resistance test of cells 6 and 7 to show why they underperformed (weak cell, damage or age)

reasoning: The onboard log in the investigation report shows cells 6 and 7 of the HLB falling below 3 V during the climb, matching the cell imbalance the operator saw. The report rules out the VTOL autopilot, motors and ESCs, and the RMA logged it as an HLB failure under warranty. Why those two cells were weak is not recorded, so the initiating cause is unknown.
notes: No Root Cause field on the ticket; the cause is in the attached report. The operator says the left lift boom snapped, but the RMA quote replaces the right lift boom assembly. The report gives both 60 ft and 80 ft for the event altitude. RMA-944/945 descriptions mix the 547 and 533 narratives. The duplicate report PDFs in RMA-945 were taken as the same content as the ticket's report (same file name and size); intake PDFs have no text.

event: On the AC 945 avionics box the PPS2 pulse from the GNSS board to the Novatel/MCM measured only 0 to 1.8 V; replacing the GNSS board fixed PPS2, but a separate erratic MCM GPIO 12 line remained under investigation.
failure_mode: PPS2 output reached only 1.8 V instead of 3.3 V (correct 1 Hz frequency), independent of harness and with the MCM disconnected
contributing: FOD (Loctite flakes, loose washer) in the avionics box
loose Novatel-GNSS board stack with a broken standoff
3.3 V DC offset between MCM ground and Novatel/GNSS ground
MCM GPIO 12 erratic with open protection diode, recurring after Hadron carrier board replacement

evidence.quote: PPS2 continues to measures 1.8V peak to peak even when harnesses are changed and when GNSS is disconnected from MCM board.
After this, the PPS2 measured normally at 0 to 3.3V peak to peak.
There is a 3.3V DC voltage between MCM ground and Novatel/GNSS ground.
The protection diode between the gpio and GND was found to be open.
With the fresh Hadron board, the MCM_GPIO_12 pin is exhibiting the same behavior as before.

would_settle_it.what: MCM GPIO 12 waveform with the fresh Hadron board, to see whether a common upstream cause (ground offset) also damaged the GNSS PPS2 output
component-level check of the PPS2 driver to find the failed part

reasoning: PPS2 stayed at 1.8 V peak to peak through harness changes and with the GNSS disconnected from the MCM, and went to the correct 0 to 3.3 V once the GNSS board was replaced, a direct swap test. A second fault on MCM GPIO 12 came back on a fresh Hadron board, and a 3.3 V ground offset between boards was measured, so an upstream cause that damaged the GNSS output cannot be ruled out; confidence is medium.
notes: Ticket closed while the GPIO 12 investigation was described as ongoing. The plan mentions harness 2121781-01 but the comment replaces harness 2121520-01. Images were not converted.

event: VXE 897 (USSS) was commanded Land Now, the operator paused the descent and micro-nudged in hover for close to two minutes, the lift battery was exhausted and the aircraft fell vertically onto a vehicle and the ground.
component: Land Now command with prolonged paused VTOL hover and micro-nudge
failure_mode: lift energy exhausted during prolonged hover while repositioning, leading to loss of lift and uncontrolled vertical descent
contributing: landing area under the aircraft not clear of obstacles
micro-nudge used instead of a larger repositioning command
front right ESC (motor 2) later found underperforming at RMA SCO (about 3.5 A versus 3.8 A)
no GCS log available

evidence.quote: Operator attempts manual nudge for 53.5 seconds
Aircraft Hybrid Lift Battery (HLB) is exhausted during prolonged pause
the use of the wrong repositioning command caused the VTOL flight time to exceed the battery’s capacity, leading to loss of lift power
I verified with Dave there were no faults in the info/logs we have prior to the Land Immediately command.
The Front Right ESC averaged ~3.5amps, while the other 3 ESCs were ~3.8amps.

team_root_cause:
After interviews with the operators and a thorough review of the data, it has been determined that the ultimate root cause of the incident was an uncontrolled decent as a result of battery exhaustion. However, the events leading up to the battery exhaustion are equally responsible for the overall incident. 
At some point during the flight, the operator selected “Land Now” instead of “Return to Base (RTB)”. When the operator noticed the landing area was not clear of obstacles, they paused the landing sequence and attempted to nudge the aircraft to a position where it was safe to continue the de

would_settle_it.what: per-motor current and HLB voltage during the paused hover, to check whether the front right ESC weakness found at RMA shortened the hover time

reasoning: The onboard log shows Land Now, a pause, 53.5 seconds of manual nudging and HLB exhaustion before the vertical fall, and no faults were logged before the Land Immediately command. The report rules out the VTOL autopilot, motors, ESCs and HLB. The RMA later found the front right ESC drawing slightly less current, which was not linked to the crash, and no GCS log exists, so confidence is medium.
notes: The Root Cause field says the main battery was exhausted; the report says the Hybrid Lift Battery. The report gives the incident date as 22 January 2025 while the ticket says 2026-01-22. Operator statement of odd behavior before Land Now was never attached. RMA-918 later failed SCO with three aborted launches before passing. Only the SR008358 quote pages 1 and 2 were read in detail (rest is standard terms).

event: VXE 508 (FBI, Octopus MWIR) lost its GCS link after 1 to 1.5 hours of flight, flew its lost-comms procedure and landed, and would not reconnect until the next morning; the cause was the user's GCS laptop with WiFi enabled sending traffic on the wrong port.
failure_mode: GCS traffic routed out the wrong network port, so the GCS could not connect to the aircraft though the radios were linked
contributing: jerky MWIR video and high data rate on the link before the loss

evidence.quote: Spoke with customer, user had WIFI enabled, and traffic on wrong port
The bird executed its loss comms procedure and landed.
This morning we hooked the bird back up to power, utilized the same GCS and same radio as last night and it connected fine and dumped the FDR
This is unrelated to our other issues.

team_view_in_comments: Spoke with customer, user had WIFI enabled, and traffic on wrong port

would_settle_it.what: XCOMM and GCS link logs at the signal degradation message to confirm the aircraft side stayed healthy

reasoning: The radios stayed linked and video was still received, yet two GCS laptops could not connect, which points at the ground network rather than the aircraft. The aircraft flew its lost-link procedure as designed. Global Support later found the user had WiFi enabled and traffic going to the wrong port, but this rests on a conversation, not on logs, so it is narrowed.
notes: The attached AAR is dated 2026-02-25, which may not be the incident flight. The second GCS also failed to connect, which the WiFi explanation covers only if both laptops were set up the same way.

event: On VXE-933 (MOLSON) the launch wizard repeatedly showed the 'one or more sensors have failed' popup and the flight was abandoned; later review found abnormal airspeed readings like those on the VXE 932 crash, which used 933's center wing.
component: air data (airspeed) measurement on the 933 center wing
failure_mode: erratic airspeed readings preflight, tripping the VTOL sensor health check; NovAtel heading disagreement is the alternative
contributing: NovAtel heading disagreement with the autopilots in software 6.6.1 (VXEP-1547), fixed in 6.7.1
fuselages and center wings mixed between 932 and 933
operators clicked through repeated sensor failure popups

evidence.quote: AAR in this ticket (1774) shows similar characteristics of 1989. Abnormal airspeed indications preflight and during launch.
thanks - yes looks like these two airplanes were mixing/matching center wings and fuselages.
The airspeed measurement is varying pretty wildly during preflight, and then shortly after transition the airspeed measurement goes to 0.
VXE 932 fuselage with 933 center wing failed to transition to FW flight.
the ‘vtol sensor failures’ are caused by a disagreement between the novatel heading and the fwap/vtol ap.

team_root_cause: SW issues in 6.6.1 will be addressed in 6.7.1
disagreement: The Root Cause field blames 6.6.1 software (the heading issue), but Cody Smisek found the 933 AAR shows "Abnormal airspeed indications preflight and during launch." like the VXE 932 crash, and Eric Brewer agreed the aircraft were "mixing/matching center wings and fuselages". The 932 crash used the 933 center wing and showed erratic airspeed, which points at the air data on that center wing rather than heading software.

would_settle_it.what: the airspeed trace from the 933 AAR preflight and launch compared with the 932 crash
which check tripped the sensor fault (heading disagreement versus airspeed) and the airspeed readings
final root cause of the 932 crash with the 933 center wing

reasoning: The ticket was first tied to the known NovAtel heading disagreement in VXEP-1547 and closed out on the 6.7.1 software fix. Later review found abnormal airspeed in the 933 AAR, and the 933 center wing then flew on the 932 fuselage in a crash where erratic airspeed preceded the loss. This points at the 933 center wing air data, but neither cause is confirmed and the center wing was destroyed.
notes: Customer quote suggests the same fault on aircraft 930 (VXEP-1547). Troubleshooting steps given to the customer were not carried out. VXEP-1989 is still open (D2). Images not converted.
